html:
Pagan was the first kingdom to unite the lands that became Burma (Myanmar), ruling the Irrawaddy valley from its capital at Pagan, now Bagan. It grew from a small settlement founded by Burman speakers in the 9th century and became an empire after 1044.

The Mranma, ancestors of the Bamar, came south into the dry zone of Upper Burma and settled among the older Pyu cities. For two centuries Pagan was one small principality among many. Then Anawrahta, king from 1044, unified the Irrawaddy valley, took the Mon city of Thaton in the south, and built weirs and canals that made the land around Kyaukse a rice bowl. He made Theravada Buddhism the faith of the state.

Its golden age followed:

  • More than 2,000 temples and stupas still stand on the plain at Bagan, out of over ten thousand built in two and a half centuries.
  • Burmese became a written language, overtaking Pyu, Mon and Pali in inscriptions.
  • With the Khmer Empire, Pagan was one of the two great powers of the mainland in the 12th and 13th centuries.

The wealth poured into temples also weakened the crown: tax-free land given to monasteries cut royal income. Then came the Mongols. Kublai Khan's armies invaded in 1277 and 1287 in the Mongol invasions of Burma, and the kingdom broke up into smaller states. Burma was reunited only under the Taungoo dynasty in the 16th century, but Pagan's language and religion lasted.
